The $12 plate that costs $16

This is one real listing, checked in September 2026. Its displayed $12 item price could not be selected without at least $4 in required choices.

Recorded 15 September 2026·Australia

On this page

  1. What the menu showed
  2. Why delivery fees are not the explanation
  3. What one listing shows

What the menu showed

On the storefront, the item appeared as a chargrilled kebab plate at $12.00, with $18.00 struck through beside it and a 33% off badge. At a glance, that is a twelve dollar meal, marked down1.

Opening the item told a different story. Choice of Preparation was marked Required, Choose 1; every option cost extra, with the cheapest at $3.00. Choice of Sauce was also required and cost at least $1.00. The required side and size choices had no-cost selections, but neither preparation nor sauce could be declined1.

At this check, no valid selection of the item produced a $12.00 item price. The required preparation and sauce added at least $4.00, making the lowest selectable item price $16.001.

The arithmetic

Advertised: $12.00. Lowest selectable item price: $16.00. The required extras add 33% to the displayed price, before a single fee is charged.

The tile also showed a 33% off badge, calculated from the displayed $18.00 and $12.00 figures1. This check did not establish the former total price with the same required choices, so it does not calculate an effective discount.

Why delivery fees are not the explanation

The usual defence of food delivery pricing is that delivery costs money — riders, insurance, support, the app itself — and that the fees at checkout cover it. Whatever you make of that argument, it cannot explain this one.

Ub*r e*ts offers pickup instead of delivery. Its fee guidance says pickup orders are exempt from delivery and service fees2. You collect the food yourself, avoiding those delivery-related charges.

Pickup does not remove the item's required $3.00 preparation choice or $1.00 sauce. Those costs remain attached to the plate1.

In our view, a $12.00 menu tile could leave a misleading impression for this item as configured at the check: even when pickup removes delivery and service fees, the lowest selectable item price was still $16.001.

What one listing shows

One listing does not establish how often this happens. It does show a specific gap: the item appeared at $12.00, while required choices made its lowest selectable price $16.001.

The ACCC says a displayed minimum price should include unavoidable extra costs, and describes gradually added charges as drip pricing3. Whether that guidance applies to these item choices, and who is responsible for the listing, still needs legal analysis.

What the evidence does not settle

This documented price gap does not establish who configured the item choices, how often the pattern appears, or whether a court would find a breach of Australian Consumer Law. The linked item may have changed since the recorded check. Readers can inspect the sources and method behind the comparison.
